proofs.proof_tex:
Fix \(P\in\mathcal P_4^{\circ}\), and put \(\delta_0:=\rho_{\mathrm{int}}(P)>0\).  The positivity of \(\delta_0\), from ass:interior-slack and def:interior-holder-class, gives two-sided slack in every density, propensity, event-hazard, residual, and H\"older-radius restriction that will be perturbed below.  The identifying functional supplied in the setup is
\[
 \theta(P)=E_P\{m_1(X)-m_0(X)\}. \tag{E1}
\]
By lem:endpoint-moment-envelope, \(D\in L_0^2(P)\) and \(\lVert D\rVert_{L^2(P)}^2=V_P\).

We first calculate the derivative.  The independent-censoring likelihood factorization separates the law of \(X\), the conditional law of \(A\) given \(X\), the conditional event law, and the conditional censoring law.  Differentiating these four factors shows that the score of a dominated quadratic-mean differentiable submodel is the \(L^2(P)\)-limit of sums of a mean-zero covariate score, a treatment score having conditional mean zero given \(X\), an event-martingale score, and a censoring-martingale score.  This follows directly by differentiating each conditional likelihood factor; the four summands are mutually orthogonal by successive conditional expectation and, for the last two summands, by the absence of simultaneous event and censoring jumps before time one.

For a mean-zero covariate direction \(s_X\), differentiating (E1) gives
\[
 \dot\theta_X
 =E_P\!\left[\{m_1(X)-m_0(X)-\theta\}s_X(X)\right]
 =E_P\{D(O)s_X(X)\}. \tag{E2}
\]
The last equality uses the conditional mean-zero property of each event-martingale integral in \(D\).  A treatment perturbation leaves (E1) unchanged.  Its score has conditional mean zero given \(X\), whereas the covariate part of \(D\) is a function of \(X\) and its event parts have conditional mean zero given \((A,X)\).  Thus both the target derivative and the covariance with \(D\) are zero.

Let \(b_a(t,x)\) be bounded and smooth, with support contained in \([0,1-\kappa]\times[0,1]\) for some \(\kappa>0\), and consider
\(\lambda_{a,e}=\lambda_a\exp(e b_a)\).  The event-hazard band permits differentiation under the survival integral.  Since
\[
 \left.\frac{d}{de}S_{a,e}(v\mid x)\right|_{e=0}
 =-S_a(v\mid x)\int_0^v\lambda_a(t,x)b_a(t,x)\,dt,
\]
Fubini's theorem, justified by boundedness and compact time support, yields
\[
 \dot\theta_a(b_a)
 =-E_P\!\left[\int_0^1S_a(t\mid X)H_a(t,X)
       \lambda_a(t,X)b_a(t,X)\,dt\right]. \tag{E3}
\]
The observed event score is
\[
 S_{a,b}(O):=\mathbf 1\{A=a\}\int_0^1b_a(t,X)\,dM_a(t).
\]
Put \(\sigma_1=1\) and \(\sigma_0=-1\).  Conditional independent censoring gives
\[
 E_P\{Y_{\mathrm{risk}}(t)\mid A=a,X\}
 =S_a(t\mid X)G_a(t\mid X).
\]
Consequently, the conditional martingale isometry and treatment overlap imply
\[
 \begin{split}
 E_P\{D(O)S_{a,b}(O)\}
 &=-\sigma_a E_P\!\left[
   \frac{\mathbf 1\{A=a\}}{\pi_a(X)}
   \int_0^1\frac{H_a(t,X)}{G_a(t\mid X)}b_a(t,X)
   Y_{\mathrm{risk}}(t)\lambda_a(t,X)\,dt\right]\\
 &=-\sigma_a E_P\!\left[\int_0^1S_a(t\mid X)H_a(t,X)
          \lambda_a(t,X)b_a(t,X)\,dt\right]
 =\dot\theta(b_a). \tag{E4}
 \end{split}
\]
A censoring score is an \(L^2(P)\)-limit of stochastic integrals with respect to the censoring martingale.  Equation (E1) is unchanged by a censoring perturbation, and such an integral is orthogonal to both the covariate term and the event martingales in \(D\).  Hence its derivative and its covariance with \(D\) are both zero.  Equations (E2)--(E4), followed by \(L^2(P)\) closure, prove that \(D\) represents the pathwise derivative on the locally unrestricted independent-censoring tangent space.

We next verify membership in the tangent closure, including the endpoint.  For arm \(a\), define the event-information measure
\[
 d\mu_a(t,x):=f(x)\pi_a(x)S_a(t\mid x)G_a(t\mid x)
                    \lambda_a(t,x)\,dt\,dx.
\]
The event part of \(D\) has formal score coefficient
\[
 b_a^{\star}(t,x):=-\sigma_a\frac{H_a(t,x)}{\pi_a(x)G_a(t\mid x)}. \tag{E5}
\]
The event-hazard band gives \(H_a(t,x)\le1-t\); the censoring-residual envelope gives
\(G_a(t\mid x)\ge(1-t)^2/2\); and the density, overlap, survival, and hazard bands give a class constant \(C\) such that
\[
 \int_{1-\kappa}^1\!\int_0^1|b_a^{\star}(t,x)|^2,d\mu_a(t,x)
 \le C\int_{1-\kappa}^1\!\int_0^1
          \frac{H_a(t,x)^2}{G_a(t\mid x)}\,dx\,dt
 \le C\kappa. \tag{E6}
\]
Thus \(b_a^{\star}\in L^2(\mu_a)\).  Let a smooth cutoff equal one on \([0,1-2\kappa]\) and zero on \([1-\kappa,1]\), and multiply (E5) by it.  On the resulting compact time rectangle, the primitive H\"older conditions and the positive bands make this a bounded smooth log-hazard direction.  Equation (E6) shows that its event score converges in \(L^2(P)\) to the event part of \(D\) as \(\kappa\downarrow0\).  The covariate component \(m_1-m_0-\theta\) is bounded, smooth, and mean zero; it is itself an admissible normalized covariate-tilt score.  Hence \(D\) belongs to the closure of the smooth score span.  Together with the representer property, this proves that \(D\) is the canonical gradient, with squared norm \(V_P\).

It remains to establish the local asymptotic normality premise rather than infer it from pointwise differentiability.  Take any finite collection, indexed by \(j=1,\ldots,d\), of bounded smooth covariate directions \(u_j\) satisfying \(E_Pu_j(X)=0\), bounded smooth treatment directions \(c_j\), and bounded smooth event directions \(b_{a,j}\), each supported in time below \(1-\kappa_j\).  For \(e=(e_1,\ldots,e_d)^{\mathsf T}\), write
\[
 u_e:=\sum_{j=1}^d e_ju_j,
 \qquad c_e:=\sum_{j=1}^d e_jc_j,
 \qquad b_{a,e}:=\sum_{j=1}^d e_jb_{a,j},
\]
and define the simultaneous submodel
\[
 f_e(x):=\frac{f(x)e^{u_e(x)}}{E_Pe^{u_e(X)}},\qquad
 \pi_{1,e}(x):=\operatorname{expit}\{\operatorname{logit}\pi_1(x)+c_e(x)\},
 \qquad
 \lambda_{a,e}(t,x):=\lambda_a(t,x)e^{b_{a,e}(t,x)}, \tag{E7}
\]
while keeping \(g_a\) and the conditional censoring law fixed and generating the latent event laws from the perturbed hazards.  The density in (E7) is allowed to remain merely measurable.  As \(e\to0\), all three ratios in (E7) converge uniformly to one, and composition and multiplication are continuous in the \(C^{3,1}\) norm on bounded sets.  Therefore the positive slack \(\delta_0\) makes every law in (E7), for all sufficiently small \(\lVert e\rVert\), a member of \(\mathcal P_4\): all bands and H\"older radii persist, the quadratic censoring survival is unchanged, the event hazards remain positive and bounded, and no atom is introduced.

Let \(L_e=dP_e/dP\) for one observed unit.  The conditional event-likelihood ratio is one off arm \(a\), while on arm \(a\) its logarithm is
\[
 \Delta b_{a,e}(U,X)
 -\int_0^U\lambda_a(t,X)\{e^{b_{a,e}(t,X)}-1\}\,dt.
\]
Taylor expansion is uniform because the directions are bounded and compactly time-supported, and it gives
\[
 \mathbf 1\{A=a\}\left[
   \int_0^1 b_{a,e}(t,X)\,dM_a(t)
   -\frac12\int_0^U\lambda_a(t,X)b_{a,e}(t,X)^2\,dt
 \right]+O(\lVert e\rVert^3). \tag{E8}
\]
The corresponding elementary expansions for the first two factors in (E7) are
\[
 u_e(X)-\frac12E_Pu_e(X)^2+O(\lVert e\rVert^3) \tag{E9}
\]
and
\[
 \{A-\pi_1(X)\}c_e(X)
 -\frac12\pi_1(X)\{1-\pi_1(X)\}c_e(X)^2
 +O(\lVert e\rVert^3), \tag{E10}
\]
respectively.  All remainders in (E8)--(E10) are bounded uniformly in the observed unit.  Hence the score vector has coordinates
\[
 s_j(O)=u_j(X)+\{A-\pi_1(X)\}c_j(X)
 +\sum_{a=0}^1\mathbf 1\{A=a\}\int_0^1b_{a,j}(t,X)\,dM_a(t). \tag{E11}
\]
Equations (E8)--(E10), followed by the Taylor expansion of the exponential square root, yield for any dominating measure \(\nu\)
\[
 \int\left\{sqrt{dP_e/d\nu}-\sqrt{dP/d\nu}
       -\frac12 e^{\mathsf T}s\sqrt{dP/d\nu}\right\}^2d\nu
 \le C\lVert e\rVert^4=o(\lVert e\rVert^2). \tag{E12}
\]
Thus every finite-dimensional smooth submodel used to generate the tangent closure is differentiable in quadratic mean.  After deleting any \(L^2(P)\)-linearly redundant coordinates, lem:iid-dqm-implies-lan applies to (E12) and proves that its i.i.d. local experiments are LAN with score covariance as information matrix.

We have now verified every premise of the corrected lem:semiparametric-convolution-bound: \(D\) is the canonical gradient, (E6) places it in the closure of the LAN score spaces, and an estimator regular for the full model is regular relative to each such finite-dimensional experiment.  The convolution conclusion therefore implies that every regular estimator having an asymptotic variance has variance at least
\(\lVert D\rVert_{L^2(P)}^2=V_P\).

Finally, thm:uniform-endpoint-efficiency gives, at this fixed interior law,
\[
 \sqrt n(\widehat\theta-\theta)
 =n^{-1/2}\sum_{i=1}^nD(O_i)+o_P(1)
 \ \Longrightarrow\ N(0,V_P). \tag{E13}
\]
For regularity, fix any submodel (E7) and any fixed local vector, and take its parameter equal to that vector divided by \(\sqrt n\).  These local laws remain in \(\mathcal P_4\).  Their primitive functions converge uniformly to those of \(P\); the endpoint envelope in lem:endpoint-moment-envelope and (E6) then give, by truncation and dominated convergence, convergence of their influence functions in \(L^2\) and convergence of their variances to \(V_P\).  Applying the uniform expansion of thm:uniform-endpoint-efficiency under this triangular sequence and centering at its own value of \(\theta\) gives the same \(N(0,V_P)\) limit for every fixed local vector.  This is regularity relative to all the generating LAN experiments.  Thus the displayed estimator attains the convolution bound at every \(P\in\mathcal P_4^{\circ}\), while its uniform expansion remains valid on the full class \(\mathcal P_4\).

Let \(\eta\) denote the true nuisance triple and define
\(\phi(\bar\eta;O):=\psi_1(\bar\eta;O)-\psi_0(\bar\eta;O)\).  By def:rmst-score and the definitions of \(D_a\) and \(D\),
\[
 \phi(\eta;O)=\theta+D(O). \tag{U1}
\]
We first establish score continuity at the quadratic endpoint.  Suppose an in-band deterministic triple \(\bar\eta\) has each of its three primitive sup-norm errors at most \(e\).  Since both hazards are in \([1/2,2]\), the identity
\[
 H_a(t,x)=\int_t^1\exp\!\left\{-\int_t^v\lambda_a(s,x)\,ds\right\}dv
\]
and the mean-value theorem give
\[
 |\bar H_a(t,x)-H_a(t,x)|
 \le e\int_t^1(v-t)\,dv
 =\frac12e(1-t)^2,
 \qquad |\bar m_a(x)-m_a(x)|\le Ce. \tag{U2}
\]
The treatment-overlap and censoring-residual bands, together with
\(H_a(t,x)\le1-t\), now imply
\[
 \left|\frac{\bar H_a}{\bar G_a}-\frac{H_a}{G_a}\right|
 +\left|\frac{\bar H_a\bar\lambda_a}{\bar G_a}
       -\frac{H_a\lambda_a}{G_a}\right|
 \le\frac{Ce}{1-t}. \tag{U3}
\]
The same calculation controls the change in the reciprocal propensity.  With
\[
 B(O):=1+\frac{\Delta}{1-U}+\log\!\frac1{1-U},
\]
equations (U2)--(U3) and direct integration imply
\[
 |\phi(\bar\eta;O)-\phi(\eta;O)|\le CeB(O),
 \qquad
 E_P\{\phi(\bar\eta;O)-\phi(\eta;O)\}^2\le Ce^2, \tag{U4}
\]
uniformly over \(P\in\mathcal P_4\).  The second inequality follows from the endpoint calculation underlying lem:endpoint-moment-envelope: an observed event at \(u\) has density bounded by a constant times \((1-u)^2\), so the squared event term is integrable, while every finite power of the logarithmic term is integrable.  Because all fitted primitives are clipped to their known bands, the first inequality in (U4), with \(e\) replaced by a class constant, also holds off a nuisance good event.

For validation fold \(k\), let \(\mathcal G_k\) be the event that the learner trained on the opposite fold, of size \(M\), has total primitive sup-norm error at most \(Cr_M\).  Here \(|M-n/2|\le1\).  By thm:primitive-endpoint-concentration,
\[
 \sup_{P\in\mathcal P_4}P(\mathcal G_k^c)\longrightarrow0. \tag{U5}
\]
Moreover, the definitions of \(J_M\), \(h_M\), and \(r_M\) give
\[
 h_M\asymp\left\{\frac{\log M}{M}\right\}^{1/12},
 \qquad
 r_M=O\!\left\{\left(\frac{\log M}{M}\right)^{1/3}\right\}. \tag{U6}
\]
On \(\mathcal G_k\), lem:exact-integrated-drift, applied separately to the two arms, yields
\[
 \left|E_P\{\phi(\widehat\eta_{-k};O)\mid\widehat\eta_{-k}\}-\theta\right|
 \le Cr_M^2. \tag{U7}
\]

Conditional on the opposite-fold training data, the validation observations are independent of \(\widehat\eta_{-k}\).  By (U4), the conditional variance of
\[
 n^{-1/2}\sum_{i:k(i)=k}\left[
 \phi(\widehat\eta_{-k};O_i)-\phi(\eta;O_i)
 -E_P\{\phi(\widehat\eta_{-k};O)-\phi(\eta;O)\mid\widehat\eta_{-k}\}
 \right]
\]
is at most \(Cr_M^2\) on \(\mathcal G_k\).  Conditional Chebyshev inequality, (U5), and a union bound over the two folds make these centered terms \(o_P(1)\), uniformly over \(P\).  The conditional mean terms are bounded, using (U6)--(U7), by
\[
 C\sqrt n,r_M^2
 =O\{n^{-1/6}(\log n)^{2/3}\}=o(1). \tag{U8}
\]
Combining (U1) and (U5)--(U8) proves
\[
 \sqrt n(\widehat\theta-\theta)
 =n^{-1/2}\sum_{i=1}^nD(O_i)+o_P(1) \tag{U9}
\]
uniformly over \(\mathcal P_4\).

For variance consistency, fix \(p=5/2\).  Lem:endpoint-moment-envelope gives constants \(0<c<C<\infty\) such that
\[
 c\le V_P\le C,
 \qquad
 \sup_{P\in\mathcal P_4}E_P|D(O)|^p<C. \tag{U10}
\]
For every \(K>0\),
\[
 \sup_P E_P\{D(O)^2\mathbf 1(|D(O)|>K)\}
 \le K^{2-p}\sup_PE_P|D(O)|^p\longrightarrow0. \tag{U11}
\]
For the bounded truncation of \(D^2\), Chebyshev's inequality gives a bound of order \(K^4/n\); for the discarded part, Markov's inequality and (U11) apply.  First letting \(n\to\infty\) and then \(K\to\infty\) proves
\[
 n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^nD(O_i)^2-E_PD(O)^2=o_P(1) \tag{U12}
\]
uniformly.  The same truncation argument, with first powers, proves
\(n^{-1}\sum_iD(O_i)=o_P(1)\) uniformly.

On each \(\mathcal G_k\), conditional Markov inequality and (U4) imply
\[
 n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n\{W_i-\theta-D(O_i)\}^2=o_P(1) \tag{U13}
\]
uniformly; (U5) removes the bad training events.  Cauchy--Schwarz, (U12), and (U13) show that the empirical centered second moment of the \(W_i\)'s differs by \(o_P(1)\) from the empirical centered second moment of the \(D(O_i)\)'s.  It therefore converges uniformly to \(V_P\).  The lower bound in (U10) makes the deterministic floor \(n^{-1}\) inactive with probability tending uniformly to one, and hence
\[
 \sup_{P\in\mathcal P_4}P\!\left(\left|\widehat V/V_P-1\right|>\varepsilon\right)
 \longrightarrow0. \tag{U14}
\]

It remains to prove the uniform normal approximation without assuming a third moment.  Put \(Z_P:=D/\sqrt{V_P}\).  By (U10),
\(E_PZ_P=0\), \(E_PZ_P^2=1\), and \(\sup_PE_P|Z_P|^p<C\).  Thus, for every sequence \(P_n\in\mathcal P_4\) and every fixed \(\varepsilon>0\),
\[
 E_{P_n}\{Z_{P_n}^2\mathbf 1(|Z_{P_n}|>\varepsilon\sqrt n)\}
 \le C(\varepsilon\sqrt n)^{2-p}\longrightarrow0. \tag{U15}
\]
For completeness, put \(R(y):=e^{iy}-1-iy+y^2/2\).  There is a universal constant \(C\) such that
\(|R(y)|\le Cy^2\min\{|y|,1\}\).  On
\(|Z_{P_n}|\le\varepsilon\sqrt n\), this bounds the expected remainder by
\(C_t\varepsilon/n\); on the complement it bounds the expected remainder by
\[
 \frac{C_t}{n}E_{P_n}\{Z_{P_n}^2
       \mathbf 1(|Z_{P_n}|>\varepsilon\sqrt n)\}=o(n^{-1})
\]
by (U15).  Using \(E_{P_n}Z_{P_n}=0\) and \(E_{P_n}Z_{P_n}^2=1\), then letting \(n\to\infty\) and \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\), gives
\[
 E_{P_n}e^{itZ_{P_n}/\sqrt n}
 =1-\frac{t^2}{2n}+o(n^{-1}),
 \qquad
 \left(E_{P_n}e^{itZ_{P_n}/\sqrt n}\right)^n\longrightarrow e^{-t^2/2}. \tag{U16}
\]
Hence the normalized sum converges weakly to a standard normal along every sequence \(P_n\).  Because \(\Phi\) is continuous, weak convergence to it implies Kolmogorov convergence.  If that convergence were not uniform over \(P\), a violating sequence \(P_n\) would contradict (U15)--(U16).  Therefore
\[
 \sup_{P\in\mathcal P_4}\sup_{z\in\mathbb R}
 \left|P\!\left\{
   \frac{n^{-1/2}\sum_{i=1}^nD(O_i)}{\sqrt{V_P}}\le z
 \right\}-\Phi(z)\right|\longrightarrow0. \tag{U17}
\]
Finally, (U9), the positive lower bound in (U10), and (U14) show that the studentized statistic differs uniformly in probability from the statistic in (U17).  For any fixed perturbation tolerance, sandwiching distribution functions and then using the uniform continuity of \(\Phi\) proves the stated uniform Slutsky conclusion.  The support fallback has probability zero under every \(P\in\mathcal P_4\), and for all sufficiently large \(n\) the small-sample fallback is inactive.  By def:endpoint-learning-handle, thm:primitive-endpoint-concentration, and def:cross-fitted-estimator, every operation is a measurable total data map depending only on the sample and the known class constants.

added_lemmas.statement: A finite-dimensional i.i.d. parametric model that is differentiable in quadratic mean at its base law \(P\) is locally asymptotically normal there, with information matrix equal to the second-moment matrix of its quadratic-mean score.

source.verbatim_statement: Differentiability in quadratic mean of a finite-dimensional model yields the locally asymptotically normal likelihood expansion for its i.i.d. experiments.

attestation.note: Transcribed at the implication level used here from van der Vaart (1998), Theorem 7.2; the node records only the DQM-to-LAN conclusion invoked in the proof.

proposed_statement_changes.proposed: At \(P\in\mathcal P_4^{\circ}\), suppose the finite-dimensional local experiments generated by finite collections of scores from the tangent score space are locally asymptotically normal, and suppose an estimator sequence is regular relative to all those experiments. If \(\theta\) is pathwise differentiable with canonical gradient \(D\) in the closure of that score space, then every weak limit law of the centered estimator sequence is the convolution of \(N(0,E_P[D(O)^2])\) and another probability law. In particular, whenever its asymptotic variance exists, it is at least \(V_P=E_P[D(O)^2]\).
proposed_statement_changes.reason: The current dominated-differentiability and pathwise-differentiability premises do not imply the convolution conclusion. Van der Vaart (1998), Theorem 25.20, requires LAN of the local experiments and regularity of the estimator; adding exactly those premises makes the cited scalar specialization faithful without changing the efficiency conclusion.

proposed.statement: For every \(P\in\mathcal P_4^{\circ}\), \(D=D_1-D_0\) is the observed-data canonical gradient of \(\theta\) in the locally unrestricted independent-censoring model, the tangent closure generated by admissible smooth submodels has squared norm \(V_P\), and every regular estimator has asymptotic variance at least \(V_P\); the estimator in thm:uniform-endpoint-efficiency attains this bound.
proposed.justification: A Gaussian limit alone is insufficient; this result certifies that the singular endpoint score is the efficiency benchmark and that the feasible procedure attains it.
proposed.gap: Westling et al. (2024), Theorem 2, derives the survival-at-time gradient under positive censoring through the horizon, while the present gradient is the directly integrated fixed-endpoint score on a model with \(G_a(1\mid x)=0\).
proposed.consumer: The efficiency certificate lets applied analysts compare alternative adjusted RMST procedures on the correct endpoint information scale.

proposed_core_edits.reason: The revised proof establishes LAN by DQM and invokes the newly materialized theorem-level DQM-to-LAN citation, so that cited leaf must be declared as a direct proof dependency.

prose_updates.tldr: In a designed-depletion or calibrated loss-to-follow-up regime, the censoring time is the earlier of two conditionally independent continuous loss or availability times whose near-horizon survivals vanish linearly, giving the known quadratic endpoint order while leaving the smooth residual censoring law unknown. At the scientific horizon, this quadratic censoring makes the influence function for survival itself non-square-integrable, but the remaining-life factor in fixed-endpoint RMST cancels one endpoint power and leaves a finite efficiency bound. The paper constructs a total cross-fitted one-step estimator with a uniform expansion over the stated radius-20 Holder primitive class while learning the treatment propensity, event hazard, and rescaled censoring residual. At every interior law, explicit bounded smooth submodels are differentiable in quadratic mean, their i.i.d. experiments are locally asymptotically normal, and their tangent closure contains the endpoint gradient, so the estimator attains the convolution bound. Simultaneous local-cubic concentration in the last time--covariate cells gives nuisance rate \((\log n/n)^{1/3}\), and a terminal-strip Fano packing proves a matching minimax sup-norm lower bound for learning the event hazard over the same primitive class. This sharp primitive rate, exact product drift, weak \(5/2\)-moment Studentization, explicit LAN certificate, and uniform Wald coverage form the publishable kernel.

project_justification.gap: Westling et al. establish machine-learning inference for treatment-specific survival and integrated RMST under a censoring floor and high-level nuisance-rate conditions. Classical endpoint Kaplan--Meier theory permits vanishing follow-up for integrated functionals but has no conditional confounding adjustment or learned nuisance blocks. Existing local-polynomial hazard theory does not supply uniform last-cell concentration when the predictable risk set collapses quadratically, and generic convolution theory does not verify LAN for this endpoint experiment.
project_justification.fill: The project integrates the survival score before analysis, learns the smooth event hazard and \(q_a=S_ag_a\) by boundary-adaptive cubic risk-set equations, proves their terminal-cell \((\log n/n)^{1/3}\) rate without assuming it, and matches the event-hazard upper rate by a same-class terminal-strip Fano lower bound. It propagates the exact product drift through cross-fitting and proves variance consistency and a uniform Studentized limit from a \(5/2\)-moment envelope. At interior laws it also constructs the finite-dimensional smooth tilts explicitly, verifies their square-root-density DQM remainders, invokes the i.i.d. DQM-to-LAN theorem, and applies the scalar convolution theorem only after placing the endpoint gradient in the resulting tangent closure.

prose_updates.related_work: Westling, Luedtke, Gilbert, and Carone (2024) is the writing and estimation exemplar: its Introduction moves from confounding and dependent censoring to a cross-fitted doubly robust survival estimator; Theorem 4 and Supplementary Lemmas 1--3 supply the foldwise decomposition and exact drift that are adapted here. Its condition B2 requires censoring survival bounded away from zero through the horizon, and Section 5.3 derives RMST inference by integrating the resulting survival-process limit. Tian et al. (2020), Theorem A1, and Stute (1995) show that an integrated Kaplan--Meier target can retain a Gaussian endpoint limit under a weighted tail integral; they neither adjust for covariates nor estimate conditional causal nuisances. Diaz et al. (2019) establish efficient covariate-adjusted RMST estimation in randomized trials with ordinary follow-up. Cattaneo et al. (2024), Theorem 1 and Appendix A.5, provide normalized local-polynomial bases, boundary-uniform Gram control, and Bernstein covering arguments under nondegenerate i.i.d. information. Jiang and Doksum (2003), equations (2.5)--(2.8) and Theorems 3.2 and 3.4, provide the Nelson--Aalen local-polynomial algebra but restrict asymptotics below an upper boundary with positive risk. Fan and Guerre (2016) provide whole-support polynomial reproduction and boundary matrix geometry, although their smooth design-density condition must be replaced by a direct density-band sandwich. Munch et al. (2024), Theorem 9 and Corollary 13, give integrated conditional-hazard rates for highly adaptive lasso under positive endpoint follow-up. Efromovich (2024) gives sharp mean-integrated-squared-error theory for conditional hazard estimation under right censoring, not simultaneous endpoint sup-norm control. Stone (1982) supplies the classical Holder minimax benchmark but not censoring-depleted terminal information. Jing, Shao, and Wang (2003) supply the weak-moment self-normalization template, while Chernozhukov et al. (2018) supply foldwise conditioning and orthogonal product-remainder organization. Van der Vaart (1998), Theorems 7.2 and 25.20, supplies only the generic DQM-to-LAN and scalar convolution machinery; the present paper constructs the required smooth endpoint submodels, proves their DQM property, and verifies tangent closure before invoking those theorems. Searches through September 11, 2026 found no result combining fixed-endpoint causal RMST efficiency, quadratic conditional follow-up loss, primitive learned-nuisance rates, and uniform feasible Studentization.
prose_updates.honest_scope: Identification of the fixed contrast is standard. Estimation, variance consistency, and inference at the quadratic endpoint are uniform over the stated primitive class, whereas convolution efficiency is asserted pointwise at each interior law. The efficiency proof uses explicit normalized covariate exponential tilts, logistic treatment tilts, and compactly time-supported log-event-hazard tilts; it proves these paths are DQM, hence their i.i.d. experiments are LAN, and shows their score closure contains the endpoint gradient. No efficiency claim is made at boundary laws. The theorem fixes the horizon \(1\), censoring exponent \(2\), one-dimensional covariate, smoothness order \(4\), and all radius and band constants. Within this class, the learned event-hazard sup-norm rate \((\log n/n)^{1/3}\) is minimax sharp; the converse does not claim a minimax lower bound for RMST risk or for each other nuisance separately. The result does not cover an estimated endpoint exponent, a shorter moving horizon, a parametric hazard subclass, or a different target. As an in-class sanity check, fix \(\delta\in(0,1)\), set \(\tau:=1-\delta\), and diagnostically restrict the same factor-preserving learner and score integrals to \([0,\tau]\). Every \(P\in\mathcal P_4\) then obeys \(G_a(t\mid x)\ge\delta^2/2\) on \([0,\tau]\), so the construction is compared in the ordinary positive-follow-up regime covered by Westling et al. (2024), while retaining its factor-preserving algebra. This diagnostic restriction is only a sanity check and does not change the fixed horizon-\(1\) target or introduce a censoring-floor assumption into the main result. The general censoring-exponent phase diagram remains a separate flagship question.

statement_notes.justification: The result now verifies, rather than assumes, the local experiment needed for the efficiency lower bound: finite collections of the smooth generating tilts have square-root-density DQM remainder \(o(\lVert e\rVert^2)\), hence i.i.d. LAN, and the singular endpoint gradient is reached by compact-time truncation in the event-information norm.
statement_notes.gap: Westling et al. (2024), Theorem 2, derives the survival-at-time gradient under positive censoring through the horizon. The present result integrates the score at a horizon where \(G_a(1\mid x)=0\), proves the endpoint tangent closure, and establishes the DQM-to-LAN premise required for the convolution bound.
statement_notes.consumer: The efficiency certificate lets applied analysts compare alternative adjusted RMST procedures on the correct endpoint information scale, with the lower bound tied to an explicitly verified local experiment.

statement_notes.justification: This is the theorem-level feasible-inference kernel: learned primitive rates, endpoint score continuity, exact product drift, weak-moment variance consistency, and uniform Studentization hold on all of \(\mathcal P_4\); the separate LAN argument is needed only for pointwise efficiency at interior laws.
statement_notes.gap: Westling et al. (2024) obtain RMST inference by integrating a survival-curve limit under a censoring floor and assumed nuisance product rates; Tian et al. (2020) treat an unadjusted Kaplan--Meier integral without learned conditional causal nuisances.
statement_notes.consumer: It supplies a fixed-horizon adjusted RMST confidence interval for the parotid-carcinoma analysis and a theoretically justified endpoint mode for CFsurvival.

proofs.proof_tex:
We prove the assertion on a finite subclass of the original model, so the resulting converse automatically applies to the supremum over \(\mathcal P_4\).  Fix once and for all a nonnegative function \(\varphi\in C_c^\infty((1/4,3/4)^2)\) such that
\[
 \lVert\varphi\rVert_\infty=\varphi(1/2,1/2)=1.
\]
For example, one may normalize the product of two copies of the function equal to
\[
 s\longmapsto \exp\!\left\{-\frac{1}{(s-1/4)(3/4-s)}\right\}
\]
on \((1/4,3/4)\) and equal to zero elsewhere.  Let \(K_\varphi<\infty\) bound all partial derivatives of \(\varphi\) through order four, with a sufficiently large fixed multiplicative constant to bound the Euclidean Lipschitz seminorms obtained from fourth derivatives.  Choose the numerical constant \(\rho>0\) so that
\[
 \rho\le \frac12,
 \qquad
 \rho K_\varphi\le 1.                                      \tag{1}
\]
This choice is independent of \(M\) and of the unknown law.

Fix a constant \(\gamma>0\), to be made smaller below, and for all sufficiently large \(M\) set
\[
 b:=\left(\frac{\gamma\log M}{M}\right)^{1/12},
 \qquad
 N_M:=\left\lfloor\frac{1}{2b}\right\rfloor .               \tag{2}
\]
Then \(b<1/8\), \(N_M\to\infty\), and, eventually,
\[
 \log N_M
 \ge \log\!\left(\frac{1}{4b}\right)
 =\frac1{12}\{\log M-\log\log M-\log\gamma\}-\log4
 \ge\frac1{13}\log M.                                      \tag{3}
\]

We first construct the laws.  Under \(P_0\), let \(X\) be uniform on \([0,1]\), let \(A\) be independent of \(X\) with \(P_0(A=1)=1/2\), set \(g_0=g_1=1\), and set \(\lambda_0=\lambda_1=1\) on \([0,1]\times[0,1]\).  Conditional on \(X\), take \(T(0)\), \(T(1)\), and \(C\) mutually independent and independent of \(A\), give \(T(a)\) event hazard one, and give \(C\) survival
\[
 P_0(C\ge t\mid A=a,X=x)=(1-t)^2,
 \qquad 0\le t<1.
\]
Extend the event hazards as one after time one and define \(T=T(A)\).  This construction verifies \(\textnormal{ass:consistency}\), \(\textnormal{ass:treatment-exchangeability}\), and \(\textnormal{ass:independent-censoring}\).  The equalities \(f=1\), \(\pi_1=1/2\), \(\lambda_a=1\), and \(g_a=1\) verify respectively \(\textnormal{ass:covariate-density-band}\), \(\textnormal{ass:treatment-overlap}\), \(\textnormal{ass:event-hazard-band}\), \(\textnormal{ass:quadratic-censoring-endpoint}\), and \(\textnormal{ass:censoring-residual-envelope}\).  The primitive functions are constant and hence satisfy \(\textnormal{ass:propensity-holder}\), \(\textnormal{ass:hazard-holder}\), and \(\textnormal{ass:residual-holder}\).  Moreover, \((1-t)^2\) is nonincreasing and tends to zero at one, and the continuous event and censoring distributions have no atom before one.  Thus \(P_0\in\mathcal P_4\) by \(\textnormal{def:quadratic-holder-class}\).

For \(j=1,\ldots,N_M\), put \(x_j:=2(j-1)b\) and define
\[
 B_j(t,x):=\rho b^4
 \varphi\!\left(\frac{1-t}{b},\frac{x-x_j}{b}\right),
 \qquad
 \lambda_{1,j}(t,x):=1+B_j(t,x),
 \qquad
 \lambda_{0,j}(t,x):=1.                                    \tag{4}
\]
Let \(P_j\) be generated exactly as \(P_0\), except that the conditional hazard of \(T(1)\) is \(\lambda_{1,j}\).  Its perturbation is supported in
\[
 \mathcal R_j:=
 (1-3b/4,1-b/4)\times(x_j+b/4,x_j+3b/4).                    \tag{5}
\]
Because \(N_M\le(2b)^{-1}\), all the rectangles in (5) lie in \([0,1)^2\), and their covariate projections are pairwise disjoint.  For every multi-index \(\nu\) with \(|\nu|\le3\), the chain rule gives
\[
 \lVert\partial^\nu B_j\rVert_\infty
 \le \rho K_\varphi b^{4-|\nu|}\le \rho K_\varphi,       \tag{6}
\]
and the mean-value theorem applied to each third derivative gives
\[
 [\partial^\nu B_j]_{\mathrm{Lip}}
 \le \rho K_\varphi,
 \qquad |\nu|=3.                                            \tag{7}
\]
Equations (1), (6), and (7), together with \(1\le1+B_j\le1+\rho\le3/2\), show both that \(\lambda_{1,j}\in\mathcal H^4_{20}([0,1]^2)\) and that its values lie in the required event-hazard band.  Every other primitive remains equal to its value under \(P_0\).  Because \(B_j\) vanishes in neighborhoods of all boundaries, extending the event hazard as one after time one introduces neither a discontinuity nor an atom.  Therefore every condition defining \(\mathcal P_4\) is satisfied and
\[
 P_j\in\mathcal P_4,
 \qquad j=1,\ldots,N_M.                                    \tag{8}
\]
At \((t,x)=(1-b/2,x_j+b/2)\), the function \(B_j\) equals \(\rho b^4\), whereas \(B_k\) vanishes for \(k\ne j\).  Hence
\[
 d(\lambda_j,\lambda_k)
 :=\max_{a\in\{0,1\}}\lVert\lambda_{a,j}-\lambda_{a,k}\rVert_\infty
 \ge \rho b^4,
 \qquad j\ne k.                                            \tag{9}
\]

We next bound the information in the observed experiment.  Only observations with \(A=1\) contribute to the likelihood ratio.  Conditional on \((A=1,X=x)\), direct division of the event density \(S_{1,j}(u\mid x)G_1(u\mid x)\lambda_{1,j}(u,x)\) and of the censoring density \(S_{1,j}(u\mid x)\{-dG_1(u\mid x)\}\) by their respective baseline densities gives
\[
 \log\frac{dP_j}{dP_0}(U,\Delta\mid A=1,X=x)
 =\Delta\log\{1+B_j(U,x)\}-\int_0^U B_j(t,x)\,dt.          \tag{10}
\]
Under \(P_j\), conditional independent censoring and the hazard construction imply
\[
 P_j(U\ge t\mid A=1,X=x)=S_{1,j}(t\mid x)G_1(t\mid x),     \tag{11}
\]
and the event subdistribution has density
\[
 S_{1,j}(t\mid x)G_1(t\mid x)\{1+B_j(t,x)\}.
\]
Taking the \(P_j\)-expectation of (10), using (11), Tonelli's theorem for the nonnegative terms, \(P_j(A=1)=1/2\), and \(f=1\), yields the exact identity
\[
 \begin{split}
 \operatorname{KL}(P_j,P_0)
 ={}&\frac12\int_0^1\!\int_0^1
 S_{1,j}(t\mid x)G_1(t\mid x)\\
 &\quad\times\bigl[\{1+B_j(t,x)\}\log\{1+B_j(t,x)\}-B_j(t,x)\bigr]\,dt\,dx.
 \end{split}                                                 \tag{12}
\]
For \(0\le y\le1/2\), Taylor's theorem and the bound \(d^2\{(1+y)\log(1+y)-y\}/dy^2=(1+y)^{-1}\le1\) give
\[
 0\le(1+y)\log(1+y)-y\le\frac{y^2}{2}.                    \tag{13}
\]
On \(\mathcal R_j\), one has \(G_1(t\mid x)=(1-t)^2\le b^2\), \(S_{1,j}(t\mid x)\le1\), \(B_j(t,x)^2\le\rho^2b^8\), and \(\operatorname{Leb}(\mathcal R_j)\le b^2\).  Combining these facts with (12)--(13) gives a fixed constant \(C_0<\infty\) such that
\[
 \operatorname{KL}(P_j,P_0)\le C_0b^{12}.                   \tag{14}
\]
Writing the product likelihood ratio as the product of its \(M\) one-observation factors and taking expectation proves additivity of relative entropy here, and hence, by (2),
\[
 \operatorname{KL}(P_j^{\otimes M},P_0^{\otimes M})
 =M\operatorname{KL}(P_j,P_0)
 \le C_0Mb^{12}=C_0\gamma\log M.                            \tag{15}
\]

For clarity, we now derive the finite testing inequality needed below.  Let \(J\) be uniform on \(\{1,\ldots,N_M\}\), and, conditionally on \(J=j\), let the sample \(Z\) have law \(Q_j:=P_j^{\otimes M}\).  Define \(\overline Q:=N_M^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^{N_M}Q_j\) and \(Q_0:=P_0^{\otimes M}\).  Expanding the logarithms under a common dominating measure gives
\[
 \frac1{N_M}\sum_{j=1}^{N_M}\operatorname{KL}(Q_j,Q_0)
 =\frac1{N_M}\sum_{j=1}^{N_M}\operatorname{KL}(Q_j,\overline Q)
  +\operatorname{KL}(\overline Q,Q_0).                      \tag{16}
\]
The first term on the right is the mutual information \(I(J;Z)\), while the second is nonnegative.  Thus (15)--(16) imply
\[
 I(J;Z)\le C_0\gamma\log M.                                \tag{17}
\]
For any decoder \(\widehat J=\widehat J(Z)\), let \(E=\mathbf 1\{\widehat J\ne J\}\) and \(p_e=P(E=1)\).  The chain rule for the entropy of the finite random pair \((E,J)\), the fact that \(E\) is determined by \((J,Z)\), and the fact that \(J\) is determined by \((\widehat J,E)\) on \(\{E=0\}\) give
\[
 H(J\mid Z)
 =H(E\mid Z)+H(J\mid E,Z)
 \le\log2+p_e\log N_M.                                     \tag{18}
\]
Since \(H(J)=\log N_M=I(J;Z)+H(J\mid Z)\), (18) yields
\[
 p_e\ge1-\frac{I(J;Z)+\log2}{\log N_M}.                    \tag{19}
\]
Choose \(\gamma\) so small that \(13C_0\gamma\le1/8\).  Equations (3) and (17) then give \(I(J;Z)\le(1/8)\log N_M\), and \(\log2\le(1/8)\log N_M\) for all sufficiently large \(M\).  Consequently (19) implies
\[
 \inf_{\widehat J}\frac1{N_M}\sum_{j=1}^{N_M}
 Q_j(\widehat J\ne j)\ge\frac34.                           \tag{20}
\]

Finally, fix any measurable estimator \(\widetilde\lambda=(\widetilde\lambda_0,\widetilde\lambda_1)\).  Decode by selecting the smallest index minimizing \(d(\widetilde\lambda,\lambda_j)\); this decoder is measurable because it compares finitely many measurable loss variables.  If, under \(Q_j\),
\[
 d(\widetilde\lambda,\lambda_j)<\frac{\rho b^4}{2},        \tag{21}
\]
then (9) and the triangle inequality make \(j\) the unique minimizer, so the decoder is correct.  Taking contrapositives in (21), averaging, and applying (20) gives
\[
 \begin{split}
 \sup_{P\in\mathcal P_4}P^{\otimes M}\!\left\{
 \max_a\lVert\widetilde\lambda_a-\lambda_a\rVert_\infty
 \ge\frac{\rho b^4}{2}\right\}
 &\ge \max_{1\le j\le N_M}Q_j\!\left\{
 d(\widetilde\lambda,\lambda_j)\ge\frac{\rho b^4}{2}\right\}\\
 &\ge\frac34.                                               \tag{22}
 \end{split}
\]
By (2), \(b^4=\gamma^{1/3}(\log M/M)^{1/3}\).  Thus (22), followed by the infimum over all measurable \(\widetilde\lambda\), proves the theorem with
\[
 c_0:=\frac{\rho\gamma^{1/3}}{2},
 \qquad c_1:=\frac34.
\]
Both constants are fixed using only the numerical class bounds and the fixed bump.  The subclass construction in (8) fixes \(f=1\), \(\pi_1=1/2\), and \(g_a=1\), all as legal members of the original class; hence the converse is over \(\mathcal P_4\), whose covariate density may otherwise be arbitrary measurable within its prescribed band.  Combined with the already-established \(\textnormal{thm:primitive-endpoint-concentration}\), it establishes minimax sharpness of the learned event-hazard sup-norm order, without asserting a minimax lower bound for RMST risk.
